title: Fake Merc Character Study (part. 1): Entering the Blohoverse
summary: First episode of a long 'case profile' series on fitness YouTuber Jason Blaha (nicknamed 'Bloho'/'Hemingway'), following his NetherBeast series. NH lists what he presents as Blaha's lies and exaggerations (IQ, martial arts, 5% bodyfat, 20-inch arms, huge lifts, height, bodyfat) to argue he has no credibility as a training or diet source. He uses it as a cautionary portrait of delusion and of how fitness gurus without results gain followers.

claims.claim: NH runs 'case profile' series on fitness YouTubers to educate viewers about untrustworthy individuals, not to make them suffer, so he avoids using their real names and asks viewers not to either.
NH's goal with the Blaha series is to kill any remaining credibility Blaha has among newer viewers who think he has changed; NH argues his information is still as bad as before.
NH's personal rule: there can be no forgiveness without an apology, and you cannot forget the actions of someone who tries to sweep them under the rug without ever acknowledging them.
NH frames such delusional gurus as a warning of what you can become if you let your life go completely off the rails.
Claiming to have been both obese and a champion long-distance runner in high school is contradictory; NH sees a pattern where Blaha's lies are never small but always extreme.
A kick works like a whip driven by hip rotation, so being able to box squat 500 lb has very little to do with kicking power; front kicks are rarely used because they are easy to dodge.
A common pattern among people who achieve nothing: they insist they could have been a doctor or anything else if they wanted, using it as an excuse.
'Schrodinger's genetics' is common in YouTube fitness: people claim great genetics when it makes them look good and bad genetics when they need an excuse for failing.
Eating 13 large pizzas would be over 20,000 kcal, beyond what even top competitive eaters manage, so the claim is impossible.
Blaha used a claimed 5% bodyfat as an argument for diet credibility, but photos show him never leaner than roughly NH's own level; NH estimates around 18% at his leanest.

Lift claims without any video, photo, witness or public record (600 lb squat, 500 lb reverse-grip bench, 2000 lb leg press for 20, six-plate deadlift) should not be believed; a 500 lb reverse-grip bench is near the world record held by ~300 lb men.

numbers.load: 600 lb squat, 500 lb reverse bench, 2000 lb leg press x20

claims.claim: NH says photos of Blaha's claimed 20-inch arms show synthol-filled, balloon-like arms, and that his arms were later damaged beyond repair, explaining why they are thin now.
Blaha admitted on forums to heavy past PED use and tried to act as a guru advising others on PED regimens despite a poor physique even while enhanced; NH sees this as unqualified, dangerous advice.
Even when a critic of bodybuilding says some correct things, it matters whether they come from belief or from envy and a desire for money; NH says Blaha's come from envy.

A loose tape measuring 17.5 inches around a thin arm is meaningless; a real 17.5-inch arm shows a clear biceps peak and triceps mass. NH estimates Blaha's arms at 14-15 inches despite his 18-inch claim.
Strength claims are meaningless without bodyweight: at a possible 240 lb, Blaha's lifts would be around 2x bodyweight, which NH calls atrocious after 20 years of training.
NH states his own bodyfat at the time as about 17% and estimates Blaha at a non-negotiable minimum of 25%.
A short man (about 5'7") with a small frame, narrow shoulders and wide hips cannot carry more than about 200 lb and look good.

Watching someone who just googles a topic and recites points is pointless; the same goes for science-fitness channels that simply read studies to you. You should read and interpret the research yourself.
Misinterpreting data to fit a narrative, e.g. citing Michael Phelps eating carbs all day to justify a large surplus as a non-athlete, is a red flag.

Benching for 20 years while always complaining of shoulder pain means you should have worked on mobility; poor squat depth, rounded deadlift back and no overhead lockout disqualify someone from advising on mobility.

NH's definition of an athlete: someone who puts the body they built to use in a sport or competition, and has some cardiovascular endurance; you don't have to look lean (shot putters, sumo wrestlers count).
Appetite is not an excuse for being fat: it is only a signal from your body and you can disobey it.
Wide hips are a bone-structure issue that cutting cannot fix; leaner bodies reveal the hips more, which NH thinks is why some people avoid ever cutting.
Loose skin is empty skin; if there is still fat in it, it is fat, not loose skin.
NH argues Blaha criticized the supplement industry out of jealousy, since he took a supplement sponsorship as soon as offered, and that he makes videos only for money.
Test for a guru: politely contradict them in their comments and see whether they ban you; NH says he was banned for disagreeing.
NH says he has followed Blaha since his YouTube beginnings and that this episode covers about one sixth of his material.

exercises.name: Box squat
exercises.why: criticised as irrelevant to kicking power
